summary.text: For the prime \(p=16843\), a finite modular summation gives \(\sum_{k=1}^{p-1}k^{-1}\equiv0\pmod{p^3}\); splitting \(H_{p^2-1}\) into multiples and nonmultiples of \(p\) and using \((ap+r)^{-1}\equiv r^{-1}-ap/r^2\pmod{p^2}\) then shows that \(p^2\) divides the numerator of \(H_{p^2-2}-1\). Since this numerator is \(\operatorname{num}(H_{p^2-2})-\operatorname{den}(H_{p^2-2})\), the relevant gcd is \(p^2\), giving the composite counterexample \(16843^2\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
p=16843,
\qquad n=p^2=283686649.
\]
We will prove that \(a(n)=n\), although \(n\) is composite. This disproves the conjecture.

Throughout, write
\[
H_m=\sum_{k=1}^m\frac1k.
\]
If a rational number \(x\) is written in lowest terms as \(x=N/D\), where \(D>0\) and \(\gcd(N,D)=1\), then A064169 at index \(m\) is \(N-D\). Thus, for \(t>2\),
\[
a(t)=\gcd\bigl(t,\,|N-D|\bigr),
\quad\text{where }H_{t-2}=N/D\text{ in lowest terms}.
\]

We first establish the arithmetic facts needed for the counterexample.

1. Rational congruences away from \(p\)

For a rational number \(x\), say that
\[
x\equiv0\pmod {p^e}
\]
if there are integers \(A,B\) such that
\[
x=\frac{p^eA}{B},\qquad B\ne0,\qquad p\nmid B.
\]
This is congruence in the localization of \(\mathbb Z\) obtained by allowing denominators relatively prime to \(p\).

The following elementary properties will be used repeatedly.

* If \(x\equiv0\pmod {p^e}\) and \(y\equiv0\pmod {p^e}\), then \(x+y\), \(x-y\), and every integer multiple of \(x\) are also \(0\pmod {p^e}\). Indeed, on putting the two fractions over the common denominator \(B_xB_y\), that denominator is still not divisible by \(p\).

* If \(x=C/E\) is in lowest terms and \(x\equiv0\pmod {p^e}\), then \(p^e\mid C\), provided \(p\) is prime. To see this, write \(x=p^eA/B\) with \(p\nmid B\). Cross multiplication gives
\[
BC=p^eAE.
\]
Since \(p\nmid B\), Euclid's lemma, applied \(e\) times, gives \(p^e\mid C\).

2. The two finite checks for \(p=16843\)

First, \(p\) is prime. Here is a compact primality certificate. We have
\[
p-1=16842=2\cdot3\cdot7\cdot401,
\]
and \(401\) is prime: trial division by the primes at most \(\sqrt{401}<21\), namely \(2,3,5,7,11,13,17,19\), gives nonzero remainders.

Repeated squaring modulo \(16843\) gives
\[
2^{16842}\equiv1\pmod {16843},
\]
and, for the four prime divisors \(q\) of \(16842\),
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
q&(p-1)/q&2^{(p-1)/q}\pmod p\\ \hline
2&8421&16842\\
3&5614&6422\\
7&2406&4466\\
401&42&9927
\end{array}
\]
Each entry in the last column minus \(1\) is relatively prime to \(p\). Explicit Bézout identities, which also check these gcd computations, are
\[
\begin{aligned}
8421(16841)-8420(16843)&=1,\\
3473(6421)-1324(16843)&=1,\\
-6873(4465)+1822(16843)&=1,\\
-3185(9926)+1877(16843)&=1.
\end{aligned}
\]
Consequently the standard order criterion proves that \(16843\) is prime: if \(r\) is any prime divisor of \(16843\), then the order of \(2\) modulo \(r\) divides \(16842\); the displayed gcd conditions force that order to contain every prime-power factor of \(16842\), hence to equal \(16842\). Therefore \(16842\mid r-1\), so \(r\ge16843\). As \(r\mid16843\), this forces \(r=16843\).

The second finite check is the special harmonic congruence
\[
H_{p-1}=H_{16842}\equiv0\pmod {p^3}. \tag{1}
\]
Here are exact details of that modular computation. The modulus is
\[
M=p^3=4778134229107.
\]
Every \(k\) with \(1\le k\le16842\) is relatively prime to \(M\), so it has a unique inverse \(u_k\in\{0,1,\ldots,M-1\}\), found by the extended Euclidean algorithm from
\[
ku_k\equiv1\pmod M.
\]
Split the sum of these inverses into blocks of one hundred consecutive values (the last block has forty-two values). If
\[
B_j\equiv\sum_{k=100j+1}^{\min(100j+100,16842)}u_k\pmod M,
\qquad 0\le B_j<M,
\]
then direct modular addition gives
\[
\sum_{j=0}^{168}B_j
 =406141409474095
 =85\cdot4778134229107
 =85M.
\]
Thus
\[
\sum_{k=1}^{16842}k^{-1}\equiv0\pmod M. \tag{2}
\]
This calculation uses only the extended Euclidean algorithm and integer addition; its role is to avoid constructing the enormous ordinary numerator of \(H_{16842}\).

For completeness, (2) really does imply the rational assertion (1). Put
\[
D=(p-1)!,\qquad A=\sum_{k=1}^{p-1}\frac{D}{k}.
\]
Then \(H_{p-1}=A/D\). Since no integer from \(1\) through \(p-1\) is divisible by \(p\), \(D\) is a unit modulo \(p^3\). Reducing the equality
\[
A=D\sum_{k=1}^{p-1}\frac1k
\]
modulo \(p^3\), with each \(1/k\) interpreted as the modular inverse of \(k\), and using (2), gives \(A\equiv0\pmod {p^3}\). Since \(p\nmid D\), this says precisely that \(H_{p-1}\equiv0\pmod {p^3}\).

Dividing by \(p\), we obtain the particularly important consequence
\[
\frac{H_{p-1}}p\equiv0\pmod {p^2}. \tag{3}
\]

3. Divisibility of \(H_{p^2-1}\)

We next prove
\[
H_{p^2-1}\equiv0\pmod {p^2}. \tag{4}
\]
Split the integers \(1,2,\ldots,p^2-1\) according to whether they are divisible by \(p\).

The multiples of \(p\) are
\[
p,2p,\ldots,(p-1)p,
\]
and their reciprocal sum is
\[
\sum_{j=1}^{p-1}\frac1{pj}=\frac{H_{p-1}}p.
\]
This is \(0\pmod {p^2}\) by (3).

Every nonmultiple of \(p\) in the same range has a unique expression
\[
ap+r,
\qquad 0\le a\le p-1,
\qquad 1\le r\le p-1.
\]
For each such pair, there is the exact identity
\[
\frac1{ap+r}
 =\frac1r-\frac{ap}{r^2}
   +\frac{a^2p^2}{r^2(ap+r)}. \tag{5}
\]
Indeed, putting the right side over the denominator \(r^2(ap+r)\) leaves numerator \(r^2\). Both \(r\) and \(ap+r\) are nonzero modulo \(p\); hence the denominator of the last term in (5) is not divisible by \(p\). Therefore
\[
\frac1{ap+r}\equiv\frac1r-\frac{ap}{r^2}\pmod {p^2}. \tag{6}
\]

Sum (6) over all \(a=0,\ldots,p-1\) and \(r=1,\ldots,p-1\). The first part of the resulting baseline sum is
\[
\sum_{a=0}^{p-1}\sum_{r=1}^{p-1}\frac1r
 =pH_{p-1}.
\]
By (1), this is actually \(0\pmod {p^4}\), and in particular is \(0\pmod {p^2}\).

The second part is
\[
\sum_{a=0}^{p-1}\sum_{r=1}^{p-1}\frac{ap}{r^2}
 =p\left(\sum_{a=0}^{p-1}a\right)
       \left(\sum_{r=1}^{p-1}\frac1{r^2}\right).
\]
Because \(p\) is the odd prime \(16843\),
\[
\sum_{a=0}^{p-1}a=\frac{p(p-1)}2.
\]
Consequently the preceding expression is
\[
p^2\frac{p-1}{2}\sum_{r=1}^{p-1}\frac1{r^2},
\]
which is \(0\pmod {p^2}\): all denominators \(r^2\) are prime to \(p\).

Finally, the sum of the error terms in (5) is also \(0\pmod {p^2}\), because each individual error has a factor \(p^2\) in its numerator and a denominator prime to \(p\). Thus the reciprocal sum over all nonmultiples of \(p\) is \(0\pmod {p^2}\). Adding the already treated multiples-of-\(p\) part proves (4).

4. Passing from \(H_{p^2-1}\) to the harmonic number needed by A309391

The index in A309391 is \(n=p^2\), so the relevant harmonic number is \(H_{p^2-2}\), not \(H_{p^2-1}\). We compare the two:
\[
H_{p^2-1}=H_{p^2-2}+\frac1{p^2-1}.
\]
Therefore
\[
H_{p^2-2}-1
 =H_{p^2-1}-\left(1+\frac1{p^2-1}\right). \tag{7}
\]
But
\[
1+\frac1{p^2-1}=\frac{p^2}{p^2-1}.
\]
Its numerator has a factor \(p^2\), and its denominator is prime to \(p\), since \(p^2-1\equiv-1\pmod p\). Hence
\[
1+\frac1{p^2-1}\equiv0\pmod {p^2}. \tag{8}
\]
Combining (4), (7), and (8) gives
\[
H_{p^2-2}-1\equiv0\pmod {p^2}. \tag{9}
\]

Now write the relevant harmonic number in lowest terms:
\[
H_{p^2-2}=\frac ND,
\qquad D>0,
\qquad \gcd(N,D)=1.
\]
Then
\[
H_{p^2-2}-1=\frac{N-D}{D}. \tag{10}
\]
This fraction is also in lowest terms, because
\[
\gcd(N-D,D)=\gcd(N,D)=1.
\]
By (9) and the numerator-divisibility property from Step 1, the reduced numerator in (10) is divisible by \(p^2\). Thus
\[
p^2\mid N-D. \tag{11}
\]
Taking absolute values preserves this divisibility, so
\[
p^2\mid |N-D|.
\]
It follows that
\[
a(p^2)
 =\gcd\bigl(p^2,|N-D|\bigr)
 =p^2.
\]
In numerical terms,
\[
a(283686649)=283686649.
\]

On the other hand,
\[
283686649=16843^2

after all, and \(16843>1\). Hence \(283686649\) is composite. Also it is certainly greater than \(2\).

We have therefore exhibited an integer \(n>2\) such that \(a(n)=n\) but \(n\) is not prime. This is a counterexample to the conjecture.
